Practical approaches for retrofitting plug flow digester and process control 
to maximize hydrolysis and methane yield from piggery waste 
Worakan Chetawan a, Kanyarat Saritpongteeraka a,b, Arkom Palamanit c, Sumate Chaiprapat a,d,*

A B S T R A C T   
This study demonstrates and quantifies biomethanation improvements from practical schemes of retrofitting 
anaerobic plug flow (PF) digester for piggery wastewater (1% total solids concentration). First, batch assays were 
performed to seek the optimal scenario for substrate solubilization. By regulating micro-aeration at different 
levels, results showed that ORP −420 ± 10 mV promoted maximal hydrolysis efficiency (ηH), to as high as 49.5% 
above the control (without micro-aeration). However, organics were markedly lost by over oxidation beyond the 
optimal ORP. Sub-thermophilic (45 ◦C) was also proven as effective (p ≥0.05) as thermophilic (55 ◦C) tem­
perature for hydrolysis with ηH 89% higher than that of the ambient (mesophilic) temperature. In continuous 
digestion studies, the two-stage operations, achieved by adding a pre-hydrolysis (pHY) reactor (HRT 1 day) to the 
main PF reactor (HRT 4 days), were assessed under four retrofitting schemes. Results showed incremental im­
provements of each strategy applied and suggested the best overall system configuration of pHY−420mV

1. Introduction 
In swine business, manure has been causing serious environmental 
problems in air, water and soil [1]. It has, nonetheless, been a good and 
cheap substrate for anaerobic digestion [2] where the biogas produced is 
utilized as fuel for heat and electricity generation for use in the farm or 
distributed to the grids [3]. This practice has helped reduce the cost of 
pork production and to a large degree abate the environmental impacts. 
By its treatment capability and benefit from energy recovery, anaerobic 
digesters were constructed in almost all swine farms for quite a long time 
[4]. This has brought our attention to the existing old anaerobic di­
gesters which are less effective and need an upgrade. 
Swine manure itself contains high solids, some of which are slowly 
biodegradable in anaerobic digester, such as partially digested grain 
fiber from animal digestive tract [5,6]. The concentration of this piggery 
wastewater varies from less than 1% to as high as 6% depending on the 
practice of farm management and water availability [7]. Anaerobic 
digestion (AD) process consists of four main steps i.e., hydrolysis, 
acidogenesis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis [3]. Hydrolysis, the first 
step in anaerobic digestion, is generally a rate-limiting step of AD for the 
high solids substrate [8]. This slowly biodegradable particulate could 
accumulate and form a dense layer in the digester’s sediment or floating 
crust causing a loss of its effective volume, which over time lowers its 
biogas production efficiency. This weakness can be overcome by adding 
mixing apparatus to the digester to be completely stirred tank reactor 
(CSTR). Such undertaking unfortunately adds considerable cost to the 
construction and can only be economically done in newer and larger 
scale digesters [9]. Other ways to enhance hydrolysis (substrate solu­
bilization) can be done through various pretreatment methods, i.e.,

Physical/chemical pretreatment methods often lead to increased oper­
ational costs due to an additional energy for substrate preparation 
(grinding, cutting, and milling) or chemical additions [10]. On the other 
hand, biological pretreatment by altering specific conditions or groups 
of microorganisms through augmentation or stimulation are benign and 
more economical. These include but not limit to phase-separation, 
operating temperature (utilizing waste heat), biological oxidation, or 
microbial inoculation. All of which aim to regulate the reactions and 
interactions among different groups of microbes in the mixed culture 
within the digester. 
Micro-aeration refers to the introduction of a limited amount of ox­
ygen or air into a reaction vessel with reactants. In case of AD, air could 
be injected directly to an anaerobic digester as to control the volatile 
fatty acid (VFA) accumulation. With a very specific amount of air, this 
approach was reportedly able to stimulate microbial oxidation of VFA 
and in turn stabilized methanogenic reaction [11,12]. Barati rashvanlou 
et al. [13] reported positive impacts of limited air supply 
(0.2 Lair/Lsubstrate.min) on the digestion of municipal sewage sludge that 
could promote CH4 yield by 2.2 times in batch experiment. Certain 
micro-aerated conditions had been shown to induce higher hydrolytic 
and acidogenic reactions in high solid fermentation of Napier grass and 
solid waste [14,15]. However, this strategy in continuous operation 
must be carefully administered as the methanogens are very sensitive to 
oxygen and over oxygen supply may result in aerobic oxidation. To 
regulate microaerobic condition for pretreatment, oxygen or air dosage 
has always been used. Oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) is in fact a 
direct representation of the state of reactions and could be a better 
control parameter. An ORP range under zero is often referred to an in­
termediate transition between oxidative and reductive environment that 
reportedly could improve hydrolysis of protein and carbohydrate of 
various substrates, as well as VFA production [11]. However, there are 
discrepancies on the proper range of ORP for a purpose of pretreatment 
since reaction kinetics are dependent on individual substrate charac­
teristics [15,16]. As far as we know, there is rare information on the use 
of ORP control for pretreatment of wastewaters. 
Temperature is an influential parameter for survival and prolifera­
tion of different microbes within an anaerobic digester. AD process can 
take place at different temperatures, normally classified to three ranges; 
psychrophilic (below 20 ◦C), mesophilic between 20 and 40 ◦C (usually 
35 ◦C) and thermophilic between 50 and 65 ◦C (typically 55 ◦C) [17]. 
Although thermophilic condition has certain advantages especially for 
solid substrate digestion [18], to heat the entire digester to such tem­
perature is too expensive. Since enzymatic activity is highly temperature 
dependent [19], thermophilic operation give an advantage to the hy­
drolysis step in AD. Thermophilic digestion relies on energy from waste 
heat from biogas engines combined with a part of the biogas generated 
[20]. To retrofit existing unheated digester to 55 ◦C, large investment on 
reactor insulation are often too expensive with operational complica­
tion. However, our study at a pilot pig farm in Ratchaburi Province, 
Thailand, using a dual source heat exchanger system demonstrated that 
waste heats of the biogas engine from cooling water and exhaust gas 
could afford the temperature of its wastewater holding tank and plug 
flow digester to a sub-thermophilic range, i.e., 40–45 ◦C [21]. By not 
requiring an external heating, this sub-thermophilic temperature range, 
believed to be less effective for AD [22], could provide a substantial 
benefit if able to find ways to optimally enhance degradation of this 
solid-laden piggery wastewater. It, hence, deserves a proper 
investigation. 
With existing anaerobic digesters, retrofitting can be done to up­
grade the efficiency and throughput of the system. For single-stage 
anaerobic digester, all hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and 
methanogenesis take place in a single unit. When an addition of a front- 
end reactor is made, establishing a two-stage configuration, AD process 
can be separated to hydrolysis and acid forming in the first, followed by 
methane forming in the second stage. This provides superior process 
efficiency and stability [23,24]. In the first stage, several strategies can 
be introduced to improve hydrolysis and fermentation through stimu­
lation and augmentation of microbial activity [25]. Utilization of the 
front unit could be done in several schemes and should be key for system 
retrofitting and methanation improvement. Proper approaches and 
optimization are needed for specific substrates. 
The aim of this research is to examine the strategies and retrofit 
schemes to improve biomethanation yield of piggery waste from a 
standard plug flow digester and to observe how the changes occur from 
each factor applied. Effects of oxidation-reduction control and temper­
ature to improve hydrolysis-acidogenesis efficiencies were systemati­
cally evaluated using a series of batch assays. The optimal conditions 
identified were subsequently implemented in the continuous digestion 
study. Four highly practical schemes for retrofitting the plug flow 
digester were tested to compare CH4 yield, followed by a preliminary 
cost-benefit analysis. Microbial community analysis was commenced to 
observe the changes in individual genus and main groups in AD 
pathways. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Piggery wastewater preparation 
Fresh swine manure was taken directly from a fattening unit in a 
local swine farm in Songkhla Province, Thailand, and kept at 4 ◦C ac­
cording to Methods for Chemical Analysis of Water and Wastes [26]. It 
was analyzed and used within 2 days after collection for the batch 
experiment (Experiment 1, Section 2.3). In order to determine the sub­
strate mass for use, the fresh manure was analyzed for total solids (TS) 
and volatile solids (VS) which are 253 ± 17 gTS/kgfresh wt. and 202 ± 11 
gVS/kgfresh wt. on wet basis, respectively. Elemental composition of the 
manure was analyzed as C, H, O, N and S found to be 37.3%, 5.9%, 
32.6%, 3.0% and 0.3%, respectively. Its C/N ratio of 15.5 is within a 
suitable range for anaerobic digestion. Fresh swine manure wastewater 
(FMW) was prepared by adding deionized water to the fresh manure to 
make a final TS concentration of 1% or 10,000 mg/L (VS concentration 
0.8%) in order to mimic the real piggery wastewater on farm. FMW was 
used for the batch study as described in Section 2.3 (Experiment 1). 
For the long-term continuous digestion study (Experiment 2), a 
manure wastewater was prepared as feed. The fresh manure from the 
same farm was spread on a clean concrete floor and sundried, then 
ground by a crushing machine (FnB Machinery & Solutions, SFL30, 
Thailand) to 0.2 mm. The manure powder was then dried in an oven at 
60 ◦C until constant weight. The dry manure wastewater (DMW) was 
prepared to a TS concentration of 1% for use as feed in continuous 
operation. Characteristics of the FMW and DMW; ORP, pH, NH4
+, alka­
linity, TVFA, fatty acid composition, total chemical oxygen demand 
(TCOD) and soluble oxygen demand (SCOD), are listed in Table S1 in 
Supplementary Material. The data in Table S1 are means and standard 
deviations from the samples prepared for each run during the experi­
ment (n ≥5). Hypothetical methane yield of the DMW from the 
Biochemical Methane Potential (BMP) assays at 35 and 45 ◦C were 163 
and 177 mLCH4/gCODadd, respectively. Procedure for BMP assay can be 
found in various works previously published [27,28]. 
2.2. Inoculum preparation 
The inoculum used in the continuous digestion studies (Section 2.4) 
was the anaerobic sludge taken from a full-scale plug-flow anaerobic 
digester of a swine farm in Ratchaburi Province, Thailand (N13◦23’ 
14’’, E99◦49’ 13’’) that was operated at ambient temperature 
(25–32 ◦C). The sludge was drawn from the settling zone near the 
digester outlet. TS and VS were measured and found to be 55,375 and 
42,639 mg/L, respectively. The sludge was kept in a plastic container 
and degassed by letting it self-digest the indigenous substrate, i.e., un­
digested manure, until biogas production was less than 1.0 mL/gVS 
according to Thaemngoen et. al. [27] This was done to minimize the

2.3. Experiment 1: Batch study of pre-hydrolysis on effects of ORP and 
temperature on fermentative reactions 
2.3.1. Pre-hydrolysis reactor configuration 
Pre-hydrolysis (pHY) reactor was made of cylindrical glass with a 
working volume of 5.0 L (total volume of 6.25 L). The top of pHY reactor 
was closed with a solid PVC lid which housed four ports; (1) sampling 
port, (2) thermocouple, (3) oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) elec­
trode, and (4) aeration port. The aeration port was connected to a 
diffuser submerged in the reactor. Air pump (TWIN, MEGA 6000, China) 
was controlled by the ORP controller (Cole-Parmer, 350 pH/ORP/ 
Temperature 1/8-DIN, USA) sensed by the ORP electrode installed at 
mid depth in the pHY reactor. The reactor was placed on a magnetic 
stirrer (IKA®, C-MAGHS 7, Germany) for homogeneous mixing during 
experiment. Temperature in pHY reactor was controlled by a thermo­
couple and a temperature controller (Panasonic, AKT4R112200, Japan) 
whereas a heat source was provided by heat tape (AKO, 52346, Spain) 
wrapping around the reactor. 
2.3.2. Experimental design of batch pre-hydrolysis 
This study used only FMW (TS 1%) prepared according to Section 2.1 
as substrate without any seeding in order to simulate the pre-hydrolysis 
tank on the field that receives only fresh manure wastewater (already 
containing natural live digestive microbes). Two experiments were 
carried out. The first was to determine the effects of ORP at four levels, i. 
e., natural anaerobic (no micro-aeration), −420, −360 and −300 mV. 
All were conducted at laboratory room temperature 28–30 ◦C. ORP was 
controlled by air injection through a micropore membrane diffuser. The 
original ORP of FMW was approximately 49 ± 10 mV and started to 
decrease from the beginning to reach the designed control values of 
−300, −360 and −420 mV at 9, 10 and 14 h, respectively. From the 
beginning, samples were collected every 6 h until reaching those target 
ORP values, where another sample was collected as a starting point of 
each treatment. Then, aeration by an air pump was automatically turned 
on by an electrical relay switch circuit whenever the reactor ORP was 
10 mV below the target value. The air pump continued until the ORP 
reached 10 mV above the control value, then automatically turned off. 
During this period, the samples were collected at six-hour intervals until 
approximately 72 h in total run time. There were around ten sampling 
points in each run. 
The second experiment was to determine the effects of temperature, 
which composed of four treatments at 30, 35, 45 and 55 ◦C. All were run 
at a fixed ORP of −420 ± 10 mV, which was identified as the best 
condition from the preceding experiment. Each pHY reactor was heated 
to its respective temperature within 10 min while ORP was continuously 
monitored. Similarly, the samples were taken every 6 h from the 
beginning and at the point when ORP reached −420 mV (at hour 14), 
then at an interval of 6 h afterwards. There were ten sampling time 
points in total at 0, 6, 12, 14, 20, 26, 38, 50, 62 and 74 h. 
2.4. Experiment 2: Continuous digestion studies on effects of phase 
separation, pre-hydrolysis, digestion temperature, and sludge re-hydrolysis 
2.4.1. System configuration 
The reactor systems operated in this study were in either single-stage 
or two-stage configuration. In the single-stage configuration, only an 
anaerobic plug flow (PF) reactor was run whereas a pHY reactor was 
added as a front-end unit in the two-stage configuration setup. There 
were two identical reactor systems operated in parallel according to the 
conditions stated in Table 1 as single-stage (PF1 and PF2) and two-stage 
(pHY1 + PF1 and pHY2 + PF2) (Fig. 1). The pre-hydrolysis (pHY) 
reactor has a configuration and accessories as earlier described in Sec­
tion 2.3.1 but with a smaller effective volume of 1.5 L. PF reactor was 
made of transparent PVC, which had an internal diameter of 10.2 cm 
and a length of 85.0 cm with the total and effective volumes of 7.0 and 
5.0 L, respectively. Temperature of PF reactor was maintained by a heat 
tape connected to a thermocouple and a temperature controller. Biogas 
produced was collected in a gasbag (Tedlar®, 232-05, UK) which was 
connected to the reactor with low permeability tube (Masterflex, Sili­
cone Tubing (Platinum) L/S®25, USA). The PF reactor was installed at 
horizontally decline angle of 10 degrees to provide the sludge accu­
mulation zone. Underneath this zone, there was a sludge draining port 
that enabled sludge recycling to pHY reactor in Phase V of this experi­
ment (see Table 1). 
2.4.2. Digester system operations 
At startup, all reactors were inoculated with the anaerobic sludge 
prepared in Section 2.2 to achieve an initial sludge concentration of 
22,000 mg/L, then added DMW (1%TS) to the reactor at 25% of its 
volume per day. These PF reactors were operated at a hydraulic reten­
tion time (HRT) of 4 days corresponding to an organic loading rate 
(OLR) of 3.63 kgCOD/m3.d until reaching stable condition. This estab­
lished a baseline piggery wastewater digestion performance of the 
original PF reactor (without retrofit). Later, pHY reactor operated at 
HRT 1 day was connected to each of the two PF reactors as two-stage 
configuration. DMW was then fed to the pHY reactors instead. The 
pHY effluents were sampled for analysis, and fed to their respective PF 
reactor. The operating schemes commenced in this experiment are 
divided into five phases as summarized in Table 1. In Phase I, both 
systems were operated as single-stage whereby only PF reactors were 
run under the identical condition. In Phase II-V, the two-stage configu­

2.5. Analytical methods 
Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) were determined using 
Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater [29]. 
Samples of swine manure were dried at 60 ◦C to constant weight and 
ground for analysis of elemental composition; carbon, hydrogen, nitro­
gen, oxygen and sulfur, by dynamic flash combustion method using 
CHNS-O Analyzer (CE Instruments Flash EA 1112 series, Themos Quest, 
Italy). 
Liquid samples were measured for ORP and pH using the electrode 
from Cole-Parmer (Self-Cleaning Flat DJ/CPVC/Pt/10′/BNC, USA) and 
Mettler-Toledo (FiveEasy PlusTM, Germany), respectively. TCOD and 
SCOD were determined following the Standard Methods [29]. For 
analysis of individual volatile fatty acids (acetic, propionic, butyric and 
valeric acid) concentration, samples were filtered through a 1.2-µm 
GF/C for SCOD measurement, and through a 0.22-µm Teflon filters prior 
to injecting to the gas chromatography (GC7820A, Agilent technologies, 
USA) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) and a capillary 
column 30 m × 0.25 mm internal diameter with argon as a carrier gas. 
Alkalinity and total volatile fatty acids (TVFA) were analyzed by a direct 
titration method [30]. 
Biogas volume was measured daily using a high precision gas flow 
meter (Multi-chamber rotor, drum-type wet gas meter, Ritter, TG0/5, 
Germany). Biogas production was adjusted to STP (0 ◦C, 1 atm) in all 
experiments in this study. For methane content determination, the 
collected biogas was sampled and injected to the gas chromatography 
(GC7820A, Agilent technologies, USA) equipped with a thermal con­
ductivity detector (TCD) and a stainless-steel packed column Hayesep 
Q80/100 (6 m × 1/8 in.) using helium as a carrier gas. 
Microbial community analysis was carried out using Next Generation 
Sequencing (NGS) method. Sludge samples of 100 mL from Phase IV of 
the main reactors (PF reactor) during the continuous digestion study,

munities and presented in terms of relative abundance. Genomic DNA

Extraction Kits (Vivantis Technologies, Malaysia). PCR amplification

2.6. Calculations 
Hydrolysis and acidogenesis efficiencies were estimated based on the 
formulae adapted from Wu et al. [31]. Efficiency of the hydrolysis re­
action is represented by a relative concentration of hydrolysis products 
(soluble organics) in terms of SCOD and CH4 leaving the system to the

represented by a ratio of total volatile fatty acid concentration and CH4 
leaving the system lumped as COD to the total incoming organics, Eq. 
(2). These two terms were used to indicate the degree of the fermenta­
tion efficiency for pre-hydrolysis experiment (Section 2.3), in which 
there was no methane generation term.

2.7. Statistical analysis 
All batch experiments were conducted in triplicate where means and 
standard deviations calculated are presented and discussed. The results 
from continuous anaerobic digestion reported were calculated from data 
at stable conditions, at least last three data points of each phase. All 
means were compared to determine the effect of the independent pa­
rameters in the performed experiments at a confidence interval of 95% 
(α = 0.05) using Duncan’s new multiple range (DMRT) by SPSS software 
version 11.0. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Experiment 1.1: Effects of ORP on fermentative reactions 
Hydrolytic bacteria are mostly aerobes, or facultative bacteria able to 
respire [15,32] with no or minimal loss of carbon through complete 
aerobic oxidation. SCOD release was thus used as an indicator of 
hydrolysis. Operation at ORP −300 mV required 6 h more to reach its 
maximum SCOD release while ORP −360 and −420 mV needed another 
12 h to arrive at their maximums which are higher than that at −300 mV 
(Fig. 2a). The maximal SCOD release equivalently occurred at ORP −360 
and −420 mV during hours 22 and 26 with the values of 2293 ± 92 and 
2320 ± 80 mg/L, corresponding to hydrolysis efficiency (ηH) 0.026 and 
0.027, respectively (Fig. 2b). This is 149.5% higher than the natural 
anaerobic (control) condition. 
In the second step of AD, acidogenesis, the hydrolysates, e.g., 
monosaccharides, amino acid and SCOD, were converted to VFAs. From 
Fig. 2c and d, time to reach the peak TVFA concentration and peak ηA 
synchronized well with that of SCOD release and ηH in each of the ORP 
levels. This was due to that both reactions can be carried out by the same 
set of facultative bacteria [33]. The peak TVFA and ηA achieved were 
12.5% and 59.2% higher than those in natural anaerobic condition, 
respectively. Even the worst ηH and ηA under micro-aeration (i.e. 
−300 mV) were still 63.2% and 20.4% better than the anaerobic 
(without aeration). Distribution of individual VFA at peak (Fig. 2d) did 
not vary by the ORP level applied. However, VFA data (Fig. S1 in Sup­
plementary Material) beyond peak time points clearly showed differ­
ential disappearances across the treatments, suggesting that O2 supplied 
may have oxidative preference among the individual VFAs. Larger VFA

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the ORP control 
strategy by micro-aeration to hydrolysis and acidogenesis in relation to 
reaction time. It clearly differs from the direct micro-aeration in the 
methanogenic reactor [11] that may cause undesirable impacts to the 
methanogenic reaction by inhibiting methanogens with the oxygen 
supply was well as diluting methane in the biogas. In this present study, 
all statistical comparisons confirmed the significant improvements 
(α = 0.05) in performance of ORP controlled hydrolysis reactors under 
batch operation. Instead of the equivalent air or oxygen to COD ratio 
such as reported in Barati rashvanlou et al. [13] and Fu et al. [35], our 
method disregards such ratios but controls on the basis of redox state. 
The ORP is directly attributed to the biochemical condition that the 
facultative microorganisms’ activities and their extracellular enzyme 
production, e.g., amylase, cellulase, and protease are driven [11]. 
However, aeration beyond the optimal time led to the continual decline 
in SCOD availability signifying the loss of carbon through heightened 
respiration and complete oxidation to CO2 [33], from which it must be 
avoided. Implication of this data set lies in the application of 
micro-aeration at an existing wastewater collection tank (a tank with 
only level control) of an anaerobic treatment system in animal farms. 
Results in the next section on the effects of temperature on 
pre-hydrolysis will further our understandings on the conditional con­
trol of this wastewater collection tank and possible gain from its retrofit. 
3.2. Experiment 1.2: Effects of temperature on fermentative reactions 
Impacts of temperature on hydrolysis and acidogenesis reactions in 
manure wastewater were evaluated at mesophilic (30 and 35 ◦C), sub- 
thermophilic (45 ◦C) and thermophilic (55 ◦C) conditions under a 
fixed ORP at −420 mV (the best condition determined from the pre­
ceding experiment). It was observed that the time to reach ORP 
−420 mV was shortened at most by only 40 min, insignificant to the 
total reaction time. At 6 h of sampling interval after reaching ORP 
−420 mV, the SCOD peak time in this experiment fell on the same time 
point at 26 h from start (Fig. 3a). 
Results in Fig. 3a clearly show that SCOD release increased with 
higher temperatures. The maximal ηH in this study was 0.051, found at 
55 ◦C and 26 h from start (Fig. 3b), This ηH was higher than at 30 ◦C by 
as much as 88.9%. The underlining reason for heightened hydrolytic 
activity at thermophilic temperature is the acceleration of temperature- 
dependent enzymatic reactions acting on the surface of the swine 
manure particles [36], together with the microbial cells activity that 
induce higher release of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes [19]. More­
over, the partial modification of substrate structure, particularly the 
particulate portion, even by low-range hydrothermal treatment also 
made it more susceptible to enzymatic attacks at a more porous physical 
matrix [28]. Above those of the mesophilic temperature, ηH at 
sub-thermophilic and thermophilic temperatures yet appeared to be 
statistically similar (α = 0.05). A raise of temperature from 45 to 55 ◦C 
was not able to provide a significant benefit in piggery wastewater hy­
drolysis beside the certainty of larger investment on insulation and en­
ergy to operate a thermophilic system. This phenomenon was perhaps 
related to the nature of this piggery waste stream that is quite diluted

4. Conclusion 
Different strategies applied to piggery wastewater digestion showed 
notable improvements. Micro-aeration through ORP control was proven 
an effective means to regulate fermentative reactions. Wastewater pre- 
hydrolysis and sludge re-hydrolysis under sub-thermophilic tempera­
ture (45 ◦C) demonstrated promising results to enhance overall digester 
performance. In continuous digester operations, a combination of ORP 
control, sub-thermophilic temperature, and returned sludge achieved an 
increase in methane yield as high as 20.4%. Enlarging hydrolytic bac­
teria abundance in sub-thermophilic reactor played an important role in 
this improvement. The investment on the proposed retrofit was esti­
mated to have a payback period less than four years. The selected 
scheme is under investigation at a pilot swine farm in Thailand.
